title: Pedagogical Principles in the Online Teaching of NLP: A Retrospection
venue: Proceedings of the Fifth Workshop on Teaching NLP (NAACL-HLT 2021)
extended_summary:
This paper examines how an online Natural Language Processing (NLP) course was designed and delivered during the COVID-19 pandemic, and whether its design adhered to pedagogical principles and constructive alignment. The authors frame the problem as how to make online teaching sustainable and effective in a post-pandemic context, especially for a technical university course with both theoretical and practical components.

The intervention is a jointly taught online NLP course developed by Luleå University of Technology and Örebro University. The course used short recorded video lectures, weekly live sessions, lab sessions, a learning management system (Canvas/Blackboard), and an assessment structure based on cumulative project tasks plus an oral exam. The course was explicitly designed around nine pedagogical principles, including active cognitive processing, feedback, clarity, and supportive learning environments.

The population consisted of 24 students enrolled in a 7.5-credit NLP course in a one-year Data Science master's program, with students from academia and industry; most had computer science or engineering backgrounds, while some lacked programming experience. Evidence came from student evaluation surveys and a student-authored perspective on the course, making the study a combination of course design reflection and descriptive evaluation. The main conclusion is that the course was delivered satisfactorily online and that student feedback generally supported the authors’ claim that the design aligned with their pedagogical goals, though there is room for improvement in practical tasks, student activation, clarity, and support.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive course-design and reflection paper with no experimental or quasi-experimental comparison and no causal estimate of intervention effects. Evidence is based on a small voluntary course survey and qualitative discussion, so it does not meet credibility criteria for higher tiers.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a modestly positive course-design impact, with high student ratings on clarity, alignment, and overall impression, but it does not demonstrate measurable learning gains or compare against a baseline. Impact is therefore plausible but unclear and limited to a single course context.

finding.finding_summary: This paper evaluates an online NLP course design and reports that students rated the technical support, course clarity, and overall course experience positively. In the student survey, technical support/communication scored 4.7/6, course clarity/ILO alignment 4.9/6, and overall impression 4.6/6 among 8 respondents out of 24 enrolled students.
finding.measure: Student course evaluation survey ratings (1-6 scale) covering clarity, technical support, assessment alignment, and overall course quality

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the online NLP course could be delivered satisfactorily and may be reusable across universities, supported by student feedback and the authors' course evaluation. It highlights increased reusability of course content, collaboration between universities, and a proposed two-track course structure as institutional improvements, though these are not tested experimentally.
finding.measure: Student evaluation ratings and qualitative course design/reflection analysis

finding.finding_summary: The course is explicitly designed to promote active cognitive processing, self-directed learning, and problem solving through short videos, live sessions, labs, and projects. Student survey results suggest the intended learning outcomes were clear (4.9/6) and the course helped students achieve them (4.5/6), but the paper does not report a formal effect size.
finding.measure: Student self-report course evaluation and qualitative feedback on learning activities and intended learning outcomes
